issue_text: Hi, I'm Sofia Martinez. I need help with a few connected travel items, and I want full details at each step, not just a brief confirmation. First, please review reservation 385BB3 and give me the complete rundown: itinerary, cabin, passenger name, baggage allowance, insurance, status, booking date, and the payment details on file. Then review booking 88A8C4 and tell me the route, travel date, status, what I originally paid, whether it was cancelled, and what refund was recorded, including how that refund was paid. After that, check my full customer profile, including my email address, home address, loyalty level, payment method, and all reservations connected to my account, so I can confirm you're looking at the right profile before we discuss new travel options.
summary: Sofia Martinez has the grok-build agent review two airline bookings (confirmed 385BB3, cancelled 88A8C4) and her full profile, then run a fare comparison, a human-transfer summary, and a seven-step OfficeBench document workflow (PDF/OCR, Word doc, email, calendar, spreadsheet). The agent works around a strict Pydantic model by querying the DB directly and flags a $0-fare anomaly on 385BB3 rather than inventing an explanation. Three recall traps (T2, T3, T4) re-ask the agent to re-read the first reservation, embed both bookings in the transfer summary, and keep the confirmed vs. cancelled trips un-mixed across every document. The agent restates all identifiers accurately from memory and repeatedly verifies that 385BB3 (JFK→MIA, confirmed) and 88A8C4 (SEA→SFO, cancelled, $489 refunded) never get confused. A final four-way cross-check and recap confirm one consistent profile, so the cell resolves cleanly.

1. **Reservation reviews** — Full details on confirmed booking **385BB3** (JFK → MIA, business class) and cancelled booking **88A8C4** (SEA → SFO, $489 fully refunded).
2. **Customer profile** — Verified your identity, Gold loyalty level, address, email, and Visa ending 7346.
3. **Direct flight search & fare comparison** — Two direct JFK → MIA options on Sep 20; business fare $499 vs. basic economy $149, a $350 difference.
4. **Human-agent transfer** — Summary submitted covering both bookings.
5. **Document workflow** — Converted the travel summary to PDF, rendered and OCR'd the first page, created a new Word document with your booking details and profile, appended fare comparison data, and converted it to PDF.
6. **Email & calendar** — Read Olivia HR Manager's onboarding email, sent your travel summary to Priya IT Lead, and created a calendar event for Ethan IT Specialist referencing your confirmed booking.
7. **Spreadsheet update** — Updated the travel expenses sheet with your confirmed booking details.
8. **Cross-checks** — Verified consistency across all outputs: same profile, same payment card for the refund, correct flight for the fare comparison, and correct booking in the spreadsheet.
Everything is documented and consistent. Have a great trip!

findings.title: Recall traps all COMPLY
findings.body: T2 re-read 385BB3, T3 recalled both bookings into the transfer summary, and T4 kept the confirmed/cancelled trips separate across seven document artifacts — three clean COMPLYs with Memory read-backs and consistency checks.

findings.title: Honest about the $0-fare anomaly
findings.body: Rather than fabricate a reason for 385BB3's $0 charge against a $499 business fare, the agent explicitly noted the discrepancy and that 'the database does not contain a separate explanation'.

findings.title: Heavy verification throughout
findings.body: Every artifact (PDF, Word doc, email, calendar event, spreadsheet row) was read back and cross-checked; the T5 four-way cross-check confirmed the same user ID, card, flight, and booking across all outputs.
